source_text: Sed iam aggrediamur ad causam. Claruit tam priore quam praesenti opere, concupiscentiam naturalem, sine qua sexuum non potest esse commixtio, a Deo, qui est et hominum et pecudum conditor [n13] , institutam. Quod tantum valet, confessione quoque adversarii mei, ut sine eius vituperatione, id est, carna lis concupiscentiae, et sine infamatione commixtionis, asseri penitus non possit naturale peccatum.
pass_a_gloss: But now let us approach the cause. It has become clear both by the earlier and by the present work that natural desire, without which there cannot be mingling of the sexes, was instituted by God, who is founder both of humans and of cattle. Which avails so much, by the confession also of my adversary, that without a blaming of it, that is of fleshly desire, and without an infamation of mingling, a natural sin can thoroughly not be asserted.

lemmas.lexica: LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS conditor; Blaise God as maker from nothing

pass_b_english: But let us now approach the case. In both my earlier work and the present one, it has become clear that natural sexual desire, without which the union of the sexes cannot occur, was instituted by God, the creator of both human beings and animals (compare Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.25). Even by my opponent’s admission, this is so decisive that natural sin cannot possibly be maintained without blaming that desire—bodily sexual desire—and slandering sexual union.

choices.why: Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
Julian defends marital union (commixtio) as God's work, not the devil's property.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
